summary: Specifies a protocol for carrying Remote Procedure Call messages over transports that support remote direct memory access. It needs no change to RPC applications or to RPC itself. It replaces RFC 5666 and is updated by RFC 8797.

plainLanguage.summary: Remote Procedure Call messages can carry large arguments and results. This RFC defines how to send their headers normally while transferring eligible data directly between the peers' memory.

questions: what is a read chunk in rpc over rdma
what is the rpc over rdma inline threshold
subtitle: How RPC messages use RDMA sends and direct memory transfers to move large data efficiently.

tldr.problem: RDMA moves data directly between registered memory regions, but RPC needs rules for message framing, receiver resources and large-data transfers on this transport.
tldr.mechanism: RPC-over-RDMA adds an XDR-encoded transport header, uses credits to limit outstanding transactions, and describes memory chunks for RDMA Read or Write operations.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8166 specifies version 1 and obsoletes RFC 5666 while retaining interoperability with it. RFC 8797 later updated it.

today: RFC 8166 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017. It obsoletes RFC 5666 and has been updated by RFC 8797.

sections.title: Why RPC Needs an RDMA Transport
sections.content:
Remote Procedure Call (RPC) lets a client ask a server to execute a procedure and return results. RFC 8166 defines RPC-over-RDMA version 1, a way to carry RPC messages over transports that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), without changing RPC itself or its application protocols.

RDMA transports preserve message boundaries like UDP, provide reliable and sequenced delivery like TCP, and support separate bulk transfers into remote memory. RPC therefore treats RDMA as a distinct transport. The version remains 1 because the protocol interoperates with implementations of RFC 5666.

The RFC clarifies earlier text, removes unsupported protocol elements, explains Upper-Layer Bindings and describes the use of RPCSEC_GSS on RDMA transports. NFS is one application that can use this transport.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC-over-RDMA carries the same RPC requests and replies over an RDMA transport. It adds rules for message boundaries and direct memory transfers without changing the RPC application protocol.

sections.title: RPC, XDR and RDMA Building Blocks
sections.content:
An RPC client acts as a Requester and sends an RPC Call. The server acts as a Responder and returns an RPC Reply. Both messages carry the same transaction identifier (XID), which lets the Requester match the reply to the call.

External Data Representation (XDR) encodes data into a byte stream without depending on the sender's native byte order. Its smallest unit is four octets. A variable-length item that does not end on a four-octet boundary receives zero padding before the next item.

RDMA transports provide registered memory, Send and Receive operations, and RDMA Read and Write operations. A Read pulls data from a remote region; a Write places data in one. A receiver must post buffers before an RDMA Send arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a call and the server returns a reply with the same transaction identifier. XDR gives both sides a consistent byte format, and RDMA can move data directly into registered memory.

sections.title: Credits and Inline Message Limits
sections.content:
RDMA receivers prepare Receive buffers before a sender posts a Send. If a buffer is missing or too small, the transport connection may end. RPC-over-RDMA therefore tracks credits and inline thresholds for each connection.

A credit represents the ability to handle one RPC-over-RDMA transaction. A Requester asks for credits, and the Responder reports the number granted in rdma_credit. The Requester MUST NOT exceed the granted limit of outstanding requests, and the grant MUST NOT be zero because that would deadlock the connection.

The inline threshold is the largest message that fits in one Send and Receive. Peers do not advertise it through this protocol. At connection start, receivers must support an inline threshold of 1024 bytes, and senders must assume 1024 bytes unless another mechanism provides a different value.
sections.plainLanguage: The Responder grants a number of transactions that the Requester can have in progress. Each peer also needs to know the largest message it can send inline, with 1024 bytes as the initial supported limit.

sections.title: Chunks and Direct Data Placement
sections.content:
A sender can remove an eligible XDR data item from the RPC Payload stream and transfer it separately. That item is a chunk, and the shortened Payload stream is called reduced. An Upper-Layer Binding (ULB) specifies which data items in an application protocol are eligible; senders MUST NOT reduce other items.

The transport header describes chunks using RDMA segments. Each segment identifies a registered-memory handle, a length and an offset. A Read chunk lets the Responder pull arguments from Requester memory; a Write chunk lets the Responder push results into Requester memory.

The Requester provides Write chunks before the Responder knows the result size. It must therefore allocate each chunk large enough for the largest possible result that may use it. Each RPC program and version that uses RPC-over-RDMA needs a ULB specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A chunk moves eligible data separately from the RPC message stream. The header tells the receiver where that data is stored and whether to read it or write results there.

sections.title: Short, Chunked and Long Messages
sections.content:
A Short Message fits below the inline threshold. The sender appends the RPC Payload stream to the transport header and sends both in one RDMA Send.

A Chunked Message removes eligible data items from the Payload stream. The sender sends the remaining header and payload in one Send; the Responder uses RDMA Read to fetch argument chunks and RDMA Write to place result chunks before returning its reply.

A Long Message is used when the Payload stream exceeds the inline threshold after reduction, or has no eligible items to reduce. The sender sends only the transport header and uses chunks to move the Payload stream. For a Long Call, the Requester provides a Position Zero Read chunk. For a Long Reply, it provides one Reply chunk sized for the maximum expected result.
sections.plainLanguage: Small messages fit in one send. Larger messages use separate memory transfers for selected data or for the whole RPC payload.

sections.title: The RPC-over-RDMA Header
sections.content:
The XDR-encoded header begins with four fixed 32-bit fields: rdma_xid, rdma_vers, rdma_credit and rdma_proc. The XID matches the RPC message, and version 1 uses the value 1. These fields must keep their meanings and positions in later versions.

The procedure field identifies what follows. RDMA_MSG (0) carries chunk lists and a Payload stream. RDMA_NOMSG (1) carries no Payload stream in the Send, so a chunk list must carry it. RDMA_ERROR (4) reports a header error. RDMA_MSGP (2) and RDMA_DONE (3) are reserved and must not be sent.

The optional Read list, Write list and Reply chunk follow the fixed fields. A minimum header is 28 bytes. Changes to the XDR require a new protocol version.
sections.plainLanguage: Every header starts with the transaction ID, version, credit value and procedure type. The procedure type tells the receiver whether an RPC payload follows or must be transferred separately.

sections.title: Reporting Malformed Messages
sections.content:
A receiver checks the transport header before passing an RPC message to the RPC layer. A message shorter than the 28-byte minimum is silently discarded because its XID cannot be trusted. For other errors in a Call header, a Responder sends an RDMA_ERROR; a Requester silently discards a malformed Reply.

Error code ERR_VERS reports an unsupported version and includes the lowest and highest versions supported. ERR_CHUNK reports a header or XDR parsing error. An RDMA_ERROR is permanent and completes the transaction associated with its XID.

RDMA operational errors are typically fatal to the connection. A Requester that cannot invalidate memory after a reply must close the connection to prevent further remote access. A Responder that cannot send a reply must close the connection to signal that the reply was lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver discards messages that are too short to identify safely. It reports other malformed calls with an error message, and closes the connection when memory protection or reply delivery fails.

sections.title: Protecting Registered Memory
sections.content:
The primary security concern is protecting local memory from unauthorized RDMA access. The RDMA provider must conform to RFC 5042. Implementations should register memory only when an RPC is about to use it and invalidate the registration as soon as the operation completes, including when an RPC is canceled.

Memory handles should be unpredictable, and implementations should avoid advertising persistently registered memory. A Responder need not read unreasonably large chunks. Repeated credit violations or repeated canceled requests can also cause denial of service.

RPCSEC_GSS can provide authentication, integrity and privacy above the transport. When its integrity or privacy service is used, the sender MUST NOT reduce a Payload stream, because removing data would change the message being protected. Lower-layer protection may be more suitable when performance matters.
sections.plainLanguage: Registered memory is accessible to the remote peer, so implementations should expose it only during the related RPC and revoke access promptly. Message integrity or privacy prevents direct data placement in this protocol.
